classes.name: Healthy
classes.cause: No disease, pest damage or nutrient disorder visible
classes.summary: A healthy tomato leaf has an even green colour and none of the lesions, mines, yellowing patterns or scorched margins seen in the other classes. Good cultural practices keep plants vigorous and reduce the risk of foliar diseases.
symptoms: Even green colour across the leaf blade
No spots, lesions or concentric rings
No winding mines or tunnels inside the leaf
No interveinal or marginal yellowing, bronzing or scorch
visual_characteristics: Uniform green tissue with normally coloured veins
Intact leaf margins without browning or drying
Smooth surface free of spots, trails or dead patches
management: Grow tomatoes in full sun (at least six hours of direct sun daily)
Test soil before planting and fertilise according to the results; avoid excess fertiliser, which favours leafy growth over fruit
Water at soil level (about one inch per week), preferably in the morning, keeping leaves dry
Mulch to conserve moisture and reduce soil splashing onto leaves
Stake or cage plants, space them for good air circulation, and remove lower leaves that touch the soil
Rotate crops and include disease-resistant varieties

classes.name: Leaf Miner
classes.cause: Larvae of Liriomyza leafminer flies (e.g., Liriomyza sativae and L. trifolii)
classes.summary: Leafminer larvae feed inside the leaf, between the upper and lower surfaces, leaving winding white trails. The serpentine mines visible in this dataset's photos are typical of Liriomyza leafminers. Heavy mining can make leaves drop early.
symptoms: Slender, white, winding (serpentine) trails inside the leaf
Mines widen as the larva grows
Heavily mined leaflets show large whitish blotches
Damaged leaves drop prematurely; early defoliation can reduce yield and expose fruit to sunburn
A related tomato pest, Tuta absoluta (tomato leafminer moth), instead makes clear patch-like mines often partly filled with frass, and its larvae also damage fruit
visual_characteristics: Thin, pale, meandering lines (mines) across green leaf tissue
Trails that become wider along their length
Whitish blotches where mines merge on heavily infested leaflets
management: Inspect transplants for mines before planting and destroy any infested plants
Conserve parasitic wasps, which often control leafminers, by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides that can trigger outbreaks
Monitor leafminer activity (e.g., trays under plants to catch dropping pupae) before deciding on any treatment
In home gardens, remove older infested leaves and keep plants vigorous with proper irrigation; leafminers rarely require treatment there
Remove old plantings right after the final harvest
Confirm the pest's identity with your local extension service (e.g., Krishi Vigyan Kendra) before treating, since other pests such as Tuta absoluta also mine tomato leaves

classes.name: Magnesium Deficiency
classes.cause: Insufficient magnesium uptake: low soil magnesium, low soil pH (below 6.0), or excess soil potassium reducing uptake
classes.summary: Magnesium deficiency appears first on older, lower leaves as yellowing between the veins while the veins stay green. It is often most noticeable during heavy fruit set.
symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between the veins) starting on the oldest, lower leaves
Veins and midribs remain green
Symptoms progress from older leaves toward younger leaves
Affected tissue may later turn brown and die (necrosis)
Often most noticeable during heavy fruit set
visual_characteristics: Green veins contrasting with yellowed tissue between them
Mottled yellow-green pattern across the leaf blade
Brown necrotic spots or patches within the yellow areas in advanced cases
management: Test soil before planting (pH and magnesium); correct low pH well in advance, since pH changes take time
Confirm a suspected deficiency with a leaf tissue test during the season
Avoid excessive potassium and phosphorus fertilisation, which can reduce magnesium uptake
Where a deficiency is confirmed, apply a magnesium source (e.g., magnesium sulfate) as advised by your local extension service (e.g., Krishi Vigyan Kendra)
Similar yellowing can have other causes, so confirm the diagnosis before treating

classes.name: Nitrogen Deficiency
classes.cause: Insufficient nitrogen available to the plant
classes.summary: Nitrogen deficiency causes a general yellowing that starts on the oldest, lower leaves and moves up the plant. Growth is restricted, and severely deficient plants become pale green overall.
symptoms: General yellowing of older, lower leaves first
Younger leaves become yellowish-green as the deficiency progresses
Restricted shoot growth, a spindly appearance and stunting
Under severe deficiency, the whole plant becomes pale green
visual_characteristics: Fairly uniform pale green to yellow colour across the leaf rather than a sharp vein-versus-interveinal pattern
Lighter overall leaf colour than healthy leaves
Few or no distinct spots, lesions or mines
management: Base fertiliser decisions on soil and, where possible, leaf tissue testing
Supply nitrogen according to the crop recommendation, splitting applications through the season rather than applying it all at once
Avoid over-correcting: excess nitrogen promotes leafy growth at the expense of fruit
Quick corrective measures such as foliar nitrogen sprays exist; follow your local extension service (e.g., Krishi Vigyan Kendra) for products and rates
Several disorders cause yellowing, so confirm the diagnosis before treating

classes.name: Spotted Wilt Virus
classes.cause: Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV; genus Orthotospovirus), spread by thrips such as the western flower thrips (Frankliniella occidentalis), onion thrips and chili thrips
classes.summary: Tomato spotted wilt is caused by Tomato spotted wilt virus, the type member of the genus Orthotospovirus, which thrips carry persistently and spread while feeding. Young leaves develop bronzing and necrotic spots, and infected fruit shows chlorotic blotches, often with concentric rings.
symptoms: Bronzing on the upper surface of young leaves
Distinct dark necrotic spots that develop on the bronzed leaves
Leaves may cup downward, and shoot tips may die back
Ripe fruit shows chlorotic spots and blotches, often with concentric rings
Green fruit can show slightly raised areas with faint concentric zones
visual_characteristics: Bronze or brownish discolouration on the leaf surface
Small dark necrotic spots scattered on the leaf
Leaf blade curled or cupped downward
Early symptoms can be subtle, with much of the leaf still green
management: Plant resistant varieties carrying the Sw-5 gene where available (some virus isolates can overcome this resistance)
Use virus-free and thrips-free transplants
Monitor and manage thrips, which spread the virus
Remove infected plants early (especially at the seedling stage) and control weeds that can host the virus and thrips
Avoid planting near infected crops, and destroy old plants and volunteers after harvest
Infected plants cannot be cured, so focus on prevention and seek thrips-management advice from your local extension service (e.g., Krishi Vigyan Kendra)
